title: Physical echo state network based on the nonlinearity and dynamic response of ambipolar heterostructure transistors

paper_content.abstract: In the field of neuromorphic computing, time-series prediction poses a significant challenge to recurrent neural network architectures, often requiring task-specific customization that limit the development of general-purpose computing platforms. In this work, we implement a physical echo-state network (ESN) using ambipolar organic–inorganic heterostructure transistors to form its reservoir layer. Leveraging the ambipolar nature of the transistor, its variable-resistance region enables sparse matrix operations, while the saturation region provides tanh-like nonlinearity, making it well-suited for implementing both synaptic weighting and neuronal activation in an ESN. Additionally, its dynamic response naturally introduces temporal attributes. Thus, it can serve as a neuromorphic computing model for time-series tasks. Without the involvement of dynamic mechanisms, it is capable of performing image recognition, time-series prediction, and multimodal recognition tasks. When dynamic mechanisms are incorporated, the model achieves an accuracy of 96.98% on the MNIST handwritten digit dataset and 86.67% on the Fashion-MNIST dataset. This work offers a neuromorphic computing architecture, providing insights for tasks such as nonlinear mapping and time-series prediction.
paper_content.introduction:
With the rapid development of artificial intelligence, computer chips are increasingly presenting challenges to humanity1–5. With the advancement of manufacturing processes, the size of transistors is approaching physical limits, meaning it is difficult to increase the density of transistors per unit area6. This has led to rising chip manufacturing costs, significant heat generation, and increased energy consumption7,8. In the von Neumann architecture, the separation of memory and processor causes memory bottleneck issues. To solve these problems, neuromorphic architectures have been proposed9–11. These novel computing architectures are inspired by the human brain and train neural network in a manner that mimics brain function12–15. Recently, researchers have utilized physical devices to simulate biological synapses and neurons, connecting these devices to construct neuromorphic neural networks. These networks emulate the brain’s working mechanisms, significantly enhancing efficiency and reducing energy consumption.

In a traditional sense, physical devices have been used as synapses to implement physical weights and as neurons to perform data mapping functions16–22. Neural networks composed of these devices have significantly advanced the field of image recognition. However, there is relatively limited research on using recurrent neural networks to address time series problems. This is partly because the training process is more complex, requiring a greater range of conductive states from physical devices. To overcome this challenge, researchers have begun exploring physical reservoir computing23–28. This approach involves constructing a reservoir with memory to replace the memory units in recurrent neural networks. Previous studies have utilized the nonlinear conductive states of physical devices to capture information from time series29. While this method is effective, it also presents limitations, such as difficulties in addressing binarization and multi-bit issues. An echo state network (ESN) is a specialized type of recurrent neural network that includes a reservoir layer30–32. The reservoir layer is constructed with a sparse matrix with fixed weights and neurons, which do not require training. The data is processed by the reservoir, resulting in reservoir states with high-dimensional features. The neural network excels at time series prediction tasks and can also classify image data that has been transformed into a time series. Consequently, reservoir layers constructed with physical devices hold significant potential.

In this work, we design ambipolar transistors based on poly(3-hexylthiophene) (P3HT)–zinc oxide (ZnO) heterostructures for implementing a physical echo-state network (ESN). Serving simultaneously as synaptic and neuronal elements within the ESN reservoir, these transistors generate high-dimensional reservoir states from electrical inputs, which are subsequently classified by a simple readout layer for recognition or prediction tasks. Across diverse machine learning benchmarks, the reservoir states produced by the ambipolar ESN consistently surpass those of unipolar counterparts, highlighting the significance of ambipolar conduction in reservoir construction. We evaluate the physical ESN in both static and dynamic operational modes. In static mode, the system achieves 95.27% accuracy on the MNIST handwritten digits dataset and 86.10% on Fashion-MNIST. For time-series prediction, it delivers normalized root-mean-square errors (NRMSE) of 0.15%, 0.22%, and 0.19% along the x-, y-, and z-axes of the Lorenz attractor, respectively. In typhoon trajectory forecasting, the ESN exhibits optimal performance with a 500×500 reservoir, and attains 89.7% accuracy in multimodal classification tasks. In dynamic mode, data are preprocessed through the intrinsic temporal response of the device, embedding temporal correlations before ESN training. This approach enhances system performance, yielding 96.98% accuracy on MNIST digits and 86.67% on Fashion-MNIST. Moreover, in Lorenz attractor prediction, the dynamic mode achieves NRMSEs of 0.165, 0.28, and 0.206% across the three axes—performance comparable to that attained with a forgetting factor in conventional ESNs. Together, these results demonstrate that ambipolar transistors constitute a promising hardware platform for high-performance neuromorphic computing.
paper_content.results:
The neural network comprises three distinct layers: the input layer, the reservoir layer and the readout layer (Fig. 1a). The input layer is used for inputting data and transforming it to other dimensions. It allows the data to be fed into the reservoir layer. The reservoir is a layer constructed with a sparse matrix and neurons. It has the function of extracting features to map data to high dimensions and can also record historical information. It is responsible for outputting the reservoir states of the ESN. The readout layer is the layer that interprets the reservoir states. The reservoir states can be quickly solved through linear regression33–35. At the same time, other machine models can also be utilized for processing, such as Support Vector Machines (SVM) or deep neural networks. The cross-sectional morphology of the transistors with various thicknesses of ZnO are shown (Fig. 1b). The thickness of P3HT deposited on ZnO of varying thicknesses is almost consistent, close to 70 nm. The thickness of ZnO has a minor effect on the deposition of P3HT, and the semiconductor performance of P3HT is almost uniform. The high-resolution image shows that the thicknesses of ZnO are 17.8, 12.2, and 8.0 nm, respectively, corresponding to the n-type, ambipolar and p-type transistors. The surface morphology of the ZnO and P3HT layers of the transistors are captured (Fig. 1c). The AFM images reveal that both the ZnO and P3HT layers are relatively smooth. The root mean square (RMS) surface roughness of the ZnO layers for the n-type transistor, ambipolar transistor and p-type transistor are 935, 718 and 704 pm, respectively. Correspondingly, the surface roughness of the P3HT layers are 4.67, 3.36 and 4.12 nm, respectively.

The output performance of the transistors is illustrated (Fig. 1d). The p-type silicon wafer acts as the gate, and the 100 nm SiO2 layer serves as the gate dielectric. The ZnO layer is deposited on top, serving as the n-type channel material for the transistor. Subsequently, the P3HT layer is deposited on the ZnO layer, acting as the p-type channel material. An Au electrode is then deposited on the P3HT layer. The ambipolar transistor can transport electrons or holes depending on the applied gate voltage. For the n-type transistor, when the gate voltage (Vg) is less than 0, electrons in the ZnO layer are captured by O2− ions, and holes in the P3HT layer are released by the conjugated chain36–38. Given that the ZnO layer is 17.8 nm thick, the electron concentration is higher than the hole concentration, resulting in the transistor being in an off state. When Vg is greater than 0, electron pairs in the ZnO layer are released by O2− ions, and holes in the P3HT layer are captured by the conjugated chain. As the drain-source voltage (Vds) increases, the drain-source current (Ids) rises linearly until it reaches the pinch-off point, after which Ids tends to saturate, indicating the transistor is in an on state. Ids reaches approximately 0.93 µA at Vg = 30 V and Vds = 30 V. For the ambipolar transistor, when Vg is less than 0, electrons in the ZnO layer are captured by O2− ions, and holes in the P3HT layer are released by the conjugated chain. As Vds increases, Ids rises linearly until the pinch-off point, after which it saturates, indicating an on state. Ids is approximately −0.33 µA when Vg = −30 V and Vds = −30 V. When Vg is greater than 0, electrons in the ZnO layer are released by O2− ions, and holes in the P3HT layer are captured by the conjugated chain. Ids again rises linearly with Vds until saturation, indicating an on state. Ids reaches about 0.33 µA at Vg = 30 V and Vds = 30 V. The balanced performance of the ZnO and P3HT layers allow the transistor to exhibit ambipolar properties. For the p-type transistor, when Vg is less than 0, electrons in the ZnO layer are captured by O2− ions, and holes in the P3HT layer are released by the conjugated chain. As Vds increases, Ids rises linearly until the pinch-off point, after which it saturates, indicating an on state. Ids is approximately −0.34 µA when Vg = −30 V and Vds = −30 V. When Vg is greater than 0, electron pairs in the ZnO layer are released by O2− ions, and holes in the P3HT layer are captured by the conjugated chain. Due to the ZnO layer being 8.0 nm thick, its electron concentration is lower than the hole concentration in the P3HT layer, resulting in the transistor being in an off state. Due to the presence of traps within P3HT and ZnO, its transfer characteristic exhibits hysteresis (Supplementary Fig. S1).

In fabricating the array device, we first employed a 100-nm-thick Al2O3 layer as the gate dielectric. The array structure (Fig. 1e) and the corresponding hardware system (Fig. 1f) are shown, along with the memory characteristics of the array (Supplementary Figs. S2–S6). To further optimize device performance, we reduced the dielectric thickness to 30 nm and 10 nm (Supplementary Fig. S7). Thinning the dielectric layer effectively lowers the operating voltage while preserving ambipolar behavior. Transistors fabricated with the 100 nm Al2O3 dielectric also exhibit well-defined output characteristics consistent with their device type (Supplementary Fig. S8). To advance integration density, we further scaled the channel length down to 2 µm (Supplementary Fig. S9). With the dielectric thickness reduced to 10 nm, the device achieves an ultralow switching energy of 202 fJ (Supplementary Fig. S10 and Supplementary Table S1), providing a strong foundation for future low‑power electronics. Moreover, the device shows clear dynamic response (Supplementary Figs. S11, S12), supporting its potential in neuromorphic computing applications. Notably, the device’s transfer characteristic resembles the tanh function (Fig. 1g), enabling simultaneous data mapping and signal bounding. Specifically, in the linear region, it can perform sparse matrix multiplication, whereas in saturation, it offers nonlinearity and amplitude constraint. Its dynamic properties further introduce temporal correlation processing. Collectively, these features highlight the advantages of using ambipolar transistors to implement physical echo‑state networks for neuromorphic computing.

To demonstrate the capabilities of the physical ESN, we first conduct a letter recognition task involving six letters (O, Z, W, T, X, U). Each letter is repeated 2000 times and assigned a label from 0 to 5. The dataset is shuffled and split into 10,000 training and 2000 test samples. Letter images are flattened into time-series signals (Supplementary Fig. S13) and fed into an input layer with randomized signed weights, converting grayscale values into bipolar features. These features are then mapped to voltage inputs for a reservoir layer implemented as a 16×16 transistor matrix (Fig. 2a, b). Sparse connectivity is emulated by activating only 10% of the synaptic connections. Two key characteristics distinguish transistor-based synaptic multiplication. First, ambipolar transistors exhibit two linear regions under positive and negative gate biases, enabling a wider and more accurate multiplicative range compared to unipolar (n- or p-type) transistors, which operate in only one linear region. Second, ambipolar devices achieve balanced channel conduction through complementary ZnO and P3HT layers, mitigating the inherent conductivity imbalance of unipolar transistors. In a comparative matrix multiplication experiment (Supplementary Fig. S14), synaptic arrays encoded matrix elements as Vds (first matrix) and Vg (second matrix). Ambipolar synaptic arrays produced results closest to digital computation, outperforming unipolar counterparts (Supplementary Fig. S15).

When transistors act as neurons, their conductance characteristics and saturation behavior critically influence the reservoir. Ambipolar transistors show symmetric current saturation under both gate polarities beyond the pinch-off voltage, providing an inherent nonlinear activation function analogous to tanh. Under ±30 V time-series inputs (Supplementary Fig. S16), n-type neurons output only positive currents, p-type only negative currents, while ambipolar neurons generate balanced ambipolar responses. Consequently, reservoir states differ markedly: n-type ESNs produce outputs from 0 to 0.75 µA, p-type from 0 to –0.1 µA, and ambipolar ESNs from –0.1 to 0.1 µA (Fig. 2c). Despite these differences, all ESN variants achieve 100% accuracy in the letter recognition task (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Fig. S17). The complete system operation is further illustrated (Supplementary Fig. S18).

The MNIST datasets are used for classification39–41. These images are all 28×28 size and are fed into the physical ESN in the same way as above. 60,000 images are used as the training set, while the remaining 10,000 images serve as the test set. Thank to the inherently excellent nonlinearity of ambipolar transistors, even when performing direct image straightening, the data can be mapped to a high-dimensional space. This allows the readout layer to easily interpret the reservoir states, enabling a single-step solution with high accuracy. The ESN achieves an accuracy of 95.27% on the grayscale MNIST handwritten digit dataset and 86.10% on the MNIST fashion dataset (Supplementary Fig. S19–S23). This is not the ultimate limit of the architecture. To achieve higher accuracy, scaling up the sparse matrix size is required. Given its already high accuracy, further improvements would necessitate additional devices, introducing inherent limitations. Another method involves prepossessing the datasets with the dynamic response of the device and then using the prepossessing datasets to complete the recognition task. Since the dynamic response can provide features for the datasets, effectively adding dynamic nonlinearity, it can also yield favorable results. We further binarize the MNIST dataset and use 4-bit encoding to map the images, followed by processing with a physical ESN for recognition. Different pulse intervals in the 4-bit encoding are employed to impart more features (Supplementary Figs. S24 and S25). Information encoding is first established through a four-bit scheme (Fig. 3a). Different types of nonlinearity are achieved by adjusting the interval pulses. For example, when the interval is increased, the responses produced by the “0,0,0,0” and “1,0,1,0” encodings are different (Fig. 3b). This gives us further opportunities for exploration. When images are processed using encodings with different pulse intervals, different image mappings are obtained (Fig. 3c). When these mappings are processed by the physical ESN, they produce different reservoir space states (Fig. 3d). Both the digital dataset and the fashion dataset exhibit discrete reservoir states (Supplementary Fig. S26). However, their time attributes are incorporated due to preprocessing with different pulse intervals. This results in the potential for creating better performance opportunities. When the mappings converted from six pulse intervals are read out by the physical ESN, the accuracy reaches 96.98% (Fig. 3e). Similarly, on the fashion dataset, after dynamic processing, the accuracy also increases relatively to 86.67% (Supplementary Fig. S27), higher than 86.10%. Therefore, introducing nonlinearity and dynamic mechanisms through physical methods in MNIST dataset processing may serve as an effective approach to enhance performance while reducing computational costs.

For neuromorphic computing systems, the capability to forecast temporal and spatial sequences is essential for ESNs42–44. To evaluate this, we apply our ESN to predict the Lorenz attractor, using data at time step t as input and at t+2 as target. This task represents a second key challenge in time‑series prediction, an area where hardware‑based architectures are actively studied. We explore two training strategies. The first adopts the forgetting‑factor method commonly used in ESNs (Supplementary Fig. S28), where the factor α substitutes for explicit dynamic mechanisms. By tuning α, the physical ESN achieves normalized root‑mean‑square errors (NRMSE) of 0.165, 0.28, and 0.206% along the x‑, y‑, and z‑axes, respectively. The forgetting factor ensures continuity in reservoir states across time (Supplementary Figs. S29–S31). The second approach directly embeds temporal attributes by preprocessing the data through the dynamic response of the physical device before training (Fig. 4a). Here, training proceeds with a forgetting factor of 1, equivalent to a static mapping setup. The device’s dynamic response performs a nonlinear transformation on the Lorenz attractor, and the resulting time‑varying Ids serves as input to the ESN (Fig. 4b–d). By varying the sampling intervals during preprocessing, different dynamic features can be extracted for prediction. Though the reservoir states under this method appear discrete, they retain encoded temporal information (Supplementary Fig. S32). This preprocessing strategy yields NRMSE values of 0.165%, 0.28%, and 0.206% on the x‑, y‑, and z‑axes, respectively (Fig. 4e)—performance that closely matches, and in some dimensions slightly exceeds, that of the forgetting‑factor method. Consequently, the system achieves low prediction error and generates smooth Lorenz attractor trajectories (Fig. 4f).

The system is further applied to predicting typhoon-center imagery and trajectories. Using grayscale image sequences and longitude–latitude data from Typhoon “Kanu” (2023), the ambipolar ESN achieved the lowest image-prediction NRMSE of 10.88% and maintained balanced dynamic activity between positive and negative states even when the reservoir was scaled to 2000×2000 (Supplementary Figs. S33–S35). For trajectory prediction, the ambipolar ESN with a 500×500 reservoir best fitted the test data, notably attaining a stable latitude‑prediction error in the range of 8.34–8.46% (Supplementary Fig. S36). These results collectively demonstrate that the ambipolar ESN excels in multi‑dimensional spatiotemporal forecasting, owing to its rich state diversity and the synergistic interplay between positive and negative activations, which together enhance dynamic‑system modeling.

To further validate the multimodal classification capability of our system, we employ electrocardiogram (ECG) signals. The signals are converted into time–frequency images via short-time Fourier transform (STFT)45,46 to form the dataset (Fig. 5a). This process yields two complementary data modalities: the original 1D waveforms and the derived 2D spectrograms. Both modalities are processed independently by the reservoir, and the resulting states are classified through a shared readout layer. Recognition can be performed on either modality alone (signal mode or image mode) or on their combined representations (dual mode) (Fig. 5b). When processed by the physical ESN, the signal and image modalities produce distinct reservoir state patterns (Fig. 5c). Combining these states enhances overall discriminability. We systematically evaluate ESN performance across reservoir scales. The ambipolar ESN consistently achieves the highest accuracy in all modes: signal mode (82.80–88.38%), image mode (84.06–87.46%), and dual mode (87.62–89.77%), with accuracy generally improving as the reservoir size increases until saturation beyond 500×500 (Fig. 5d). The p‑type ESN delivers stable, scale‑insensitive performance, particularly in dual mode where accuracy remains nearly constant (87.39–88.35%). In contrast, the n‑type ESN peaks in dual mode at 87.81% with a 200×200 reservoir, beyond which performance degrades, revealing limited scalability. These results underscore the ambipolar ESN as the most robust and scalable architecture for multimodal processing, achieving superior accuracy while maintaining consistent performance scaling. This advantage stems from its more balanced reservoir state distribution across positive and negative activations (Supplementary Figs. S37–39).

Finally, a task utilizing the Mosei dataset for multimodal recognition was conducted. The audio, text, and visual features from Mosei were processed using a pooling mechanism and then classified with SVM. For tri-modal classification (Supplementary Fig. S40), the accuracy without the ambipolar ESN is 71.33%, whereas with the ambipolar ESN, it improves to 76.07%. This demonstrates that the ambipolar ESN significantly enhances the accuracy of multimodal recognition. For dual-modal classification, the accuracies for visual/audio, visual/text, and text/audio combinations are 70.86, 76.46, and 76.01%, respectively. For monomodal classification, the accuracies for text, audio, and visual modalities are 76.48, 71.01, and 71.03%, respectively. Using a 10 nm alumina dielectric layer allows the transistor array to operate at lower voltages, yet introduces process-related challenges in uniformity and endurance (Supplementary Fig. S41). When the pulse interval is increased sufficiently, the dynamic response of the array gradually transitions toward static behavior (Supplementary Fig. S42). In image recognition tasks, relying solely on the final current value after dynamic mapping proves inadequate. For instance, in 5‑bit English letter recognition using only the steady‑state response as the training feature, we observed misclassification patterns (Supplementary Figs. S43, S44), attributable to the loss of transient information. Compared to binarized inputs, conventional 4‑bit digital encoding yields lower accuracy due to feature compression (Supplementary Fig. S45). However, by fully utilizing the temporal 4‑bit response data, recognition accuracy improves from 84.92% to 87.94% (Supplementary Fig. S46), confirming that dynamic nonlinearity enhances binarized image classification. To further boost accuracy, we introduced sparse projection and activation‑based feature extraction, combining these derived features with raw data for training. This strategy led to additional gains in recognition performance (Supplementary Figs. S47–S55). The array architecture can physically implement such operations through its tunable linear regions and inherent nonlinearity, supporting efficient and accurate image recognition.

Nevertheless, while the system exhibits strong recognition capability, further accuracy improvements demand increased computational resources. Moreover, time‑series prediction currently relies on a forgetting factor, implying that the computational model must support online iteration. These limitations can be mitigated by leveraging the device’s intrinsic dynamic response. The additional features generated through dynamics enhance physical ESN performance without digital overhead. In time‑series prediction, the device’s dynamic equation mapping enables single‑pass inference, eliminating the need for online iterative updates.

In summary, ambipolar transistors, with their balanced linear characteristics and bounded output response, are particularly suitable for emulating both the linear weighting of synapses and the nonlinear activation of neurons in a reservoir layer. Since the weights in the reservoir layer are fixed and require no training, such devices represent a promising candidate for constructing recurrent neural networks with inherent dynamic constraints, highlighting considerable research potential. In contrast, p-type and n-type transistors exhibit limitations in building high-performance reservoirs due to their weaker capability to bound signal amplitudes. Under static operation, the system has demonstrated strong potential in tasks such as image recognition, time-series prediction, and multimodal classification. In dynamic mode, by leveraging the intrinsic transient response of the device, temporal correlations can be embedded into the data, leading to further improvements in image recognition performance. Particularly for time-series forecasting, the dynamic mechanism can replace the forgetting factor used in conventional ESNs, transforming iterative online computation into single-step forward processing, thereby enhancing overall computational efficiency.
paper_content.methods:
Fabrication of the device and array
The bottom gate electrodes were fabricated via physical vapor deposition. Aluminum oxide was subsequently deposited as the gate dielectric using atomic layer deposition. For the semiconductor layers, ZnO was prepared by dissolving the precursor in ammonia to form a uniform solution, while P3HT was dissolved in toluene and thoroughly mixed by stirring and heating to ensure homogeneity. The substrate was placed on a spin coater, and the ZnO precursor solution was dispensed onto it. Spin-coating was performed sequentially at 1500 rpm, 2000 rpm, and 2500 rpm, each for 30 s. After spin-coating, the substrate was annealed at 150 °C for 40 min to remove the solvent and crystallize the ZnO thin film. The P3HT solution was then applied onto the ZnO layer, with the volume carefully controlled to ensure film uniformity, followed by spin-coating at 1500 rpm for 30 s. The resulting film was annealed at 100 °C for 20 min. Device and array structures were defined by covering the thin film with a mask and depositing electrodes via physical vapor deposition. All fabrication steps were conducted in a nitrogen atmosphere. The completed array was encapsulated by covering it with a quartz glass sheet and sealing the edges with UV-curable adhesive.

Control of the array
Specific rows are selected by applying a feature signal that connects the input voltage to the drain terminals of all transistors in the chosen row via a digital-to-analog converter (DAC). Simultaneously, specific columns are addressed by applying a column selection signal to the gate terminals of all transistors in the selected column. This addressing scheme enables individual control of each unit within the array, facilitating the implementation of matrix multiplication and activation functions.

Measurement of the array
A custom program was used to sequentially access and test each node in the array, thereby evaluating the operational performance and stability of the array. To measure the output, a resistor with a known value (1 MΩ) was connected in series at the output terminal of the transistor array, allowing the output current to be converted into a voltage signal for further analysis.

Device characterization
The electrical properties of the device were tested using a semiconductor analyzer (Keysight B2902B). The device was first cutting using Focused Ion Beam Scanning Electron Microscopy (Helios 5UC 03040707), and then the cross-sectional morphology was taken by Field Emission Transmission Electron Microscopy (JEOL-F200). The surface morphology of the device was characterized using an Atomic Force Microscope (Cypher S/Oxford Instruments Asylum Research).

Equation
The formula for the status of the reservoir is given as follows:
U(t) = U(t−1)(1−α) + αtanh(Xt Win + U(t−1) Wres) (1)

Where U(t), U(t−1), α (alpha), Xt, Win, Wres are represent for reservoir state at time step t, reservoir state at the previous time step at t−1, forgetting rate, input at time step, input weight matrix and reservoir weight matrix.

The solution method for the reading layer uses the linear regression formula:
Wout = (UTU)−1(UTylabel) (2)

Wout is the readout layer matrix, U is the reservoir state, and ylabel is the label value.

The formula for the Lorentz attractor is given as follows:
dx/dt = σ(y−x)
dy/dt = x(ρ−z)−y (3)
dz/dt = xy−βz

σ, ρ and β are respectively the Prandtl number, the Rayleigh number and the geometric factor.

In addition, the gradient descent algorithm is used in the prediction of the typhoon center, with Adam as the optimizer. The loss function used is the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), and its formula is as follows:
RMSE = 1/n Σ (ylabel − ypredict)2 (4)

ypredict is the predicted result.

The formula for NRMSE is given as follows:
NRMSE = 1/(ymax − ymin) * sqrt(1/n Σ (ylabel − ypredict)2) (5)

ymax, ymin are max value of ylabel, min value of ylabel, respectively.

Dataset
The MNIST handwritten digits and fashion datasets are provided by the National Institute of Standards and Technology. Each dataset consists of 60,000 images for training and 10,000 images for testing. The Lorenz attractor curve comprises 10,000 points, with the first 5000 points used as the training set and the remaining 5000 points as the test set. In this task, the input consists of points 1 to 4998, while the target includes points 3 to 5000. The images of the typhoon center and its movement trajectory are derived from Typhoon Khanun in 2023. The ECG dataset is sourced from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology-Beth Israel Hospital, and includes 17 categories based on their annotations. To ensured dataset validity, ECG signals with more than 100 samples are selected, resulting in a total of 11,811 samples. The first 10,000 samples are used for training, and the remainder are used for testing. The CMU-MOSEI dataset, developed by the Multimodal Communication and Language Analysis Lab at Carnegie Mellon University (CMU), uses binary classification labels: 0 for values less than 0, and 1 for values greater than or equal to 0. In addition, the support vector machine employed in the final section of the study uses a linear kernel function, with the C parameter set to 0.0001.

Networks
The English alphabet recognition task and Lorenz attractor prediction are achieved through a 16×16 ambipolar transistor array, with read/write operations on the array controlled by DACs and an ADC via STM32. MNIST handwritten digits, the Fashion dataset, Lorenz attractor prediction, ECG data classification, and multimodal recognition with the MOSEI dataset are implemented using Python+PyTorch simulations. The simulation is performed by an operational model of the device. The specific physical ESN network structure is provided in the Supplementary Table S2.

Data availability
The physical data generated in this study have been deposited in the Zenodo database [https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18475506].

Code availability
The code is available at Zenodo [https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18459291].

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This paper describes the implementation of physical reservoir computing by utilizing ZnO/P3HT ambipolar transistor array as a physical reservoir. The proposed ZnO/P3HT device can be configured in either n-type, ambipolar, or p-type. The authors found that for the purpose of vector-matrix multiplication and accurate physical reservoir computing, the ambipolar characteristic is highly desirable. The single-polar n-type or p-type devices resulted in single-signed outputs, leading to limited reservoir states. As demonstrations of the approach, tasks such as letter recognition, MNIST dataset classification were done as an example of processing static data. Another set of tasks such as prediction of typhoon route or classifying ECG signals were presented as demonstrations of learning dynamic systems.

This paper reveals the importance of ambipolar properties in building neural networks, and presents a novel method of utilizing transistors for physical reservoir computing. However, most importantly, the descriptions of how the system works are unclear. I believe that they should be addressed before additional review and publication.
- It seems that a single device is used repeatedly to implement the physical array operation. Given the device structure, construction of the array is not straightforward. This should be clearly stated. I wonder if the computation is done by simulation (based on the model of the device operation), or by measuring the response from the single device repeatedly to construct the response from the array.
- What is the exact structure of the network including the reservoir? It seems that the input data scale is first reduced to match the size of the reservoir input using a single-layer neural network. Then, what does the 'step' mean in figures for reservoir state output? (Fig. 2c, 3b, 3c) Probably, the step means the sample number.
- Once again, detailed network structure for temporal and spatial sequence forecasting is not clear from the text. How is temporal data being processed?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The manuscript presents a physical Echo State Network utilizing ambipolar organic-inorganic heterostructure transistors. Key achievements include high accuracy on multiple tasks, such as the typhoon trajectory prediction. The ambipolar transistors demonstrate superior performance compared to n-type and p-type variants, attributed to their balanced conductivity and dual linear regions, enabling effective feature mapping and reservoir state diversity. This work bridges neuromorphic hardware design with machine learning applications, offering a pathway toward energy-efficient computing platforms.

The manuscript can be improved by addressing the following concerns:
1. As is introduced in the manuscript, the PRC involves constructing a reservoir with memory to replace the memory units in recurrent neural networks. It would be reasonable to discuss the memory characteristic of the devices presented. My understanding is that different from the "ideal" transistors for CMOS ICs with no or little hysteresis, the transistors developed in this work should present hysteresis in the transfer curves due to ion immigration or trap states, which can be the source of coherent memory.
2. The size of the physical reservoir, for example "500*500", is not clearly explained. Does the size of the physical reservoir correspond to the array dimensions of the devices? How are these device arrays fabricated, controlled, and measured? I would suggest that the authors provide a description of the operation of the system.
3. The writing can be further improved by condensing the manuscript.
Other suggestions for the authors:
4. The color bar is missing in several figures, such as Figure 2.
5. The text in Figure 2a is horizontal, which seems unnecessary.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In this manuscript, the authors present an ambipolar organic-inorganic heterostructure transistor with potential applications in reservoir computing systems. While various applications have been demonstrated, the work does not introduce any fundamental innovations or address key challenges in the field. Additionally, the manuscript suffers from significant issues in grammar and logical flow, which further undermine its clarity and overall presentation. The current version does not meet the standards expected of journals in the Nature Communications. Below are my detailed concerns regarding the manuscript:
1. The manuscript lacks comprehensive device testing. The authors need to provide data on endurance, retention, uniformity, switching speed, and environmental stability to evaluate whether the device is sufficiently robust and suitable for computing applications.
2. The authors mention in the introduction that transistor sizes are approaching physical limits. What is the actual size of the proposed device? Does this new design contribute to reducing transistor dimensions or increasing the density of transistors per unit area?
3. Reservoir computing typically requires specific temporal dynamics. Do the proposed devices exhibit any intrinsic temporal properties essential for reservoir computing?
4. Can the operating voltage of this device be reduced in future implementations? The authors should provide an analysis of potential strategies for lowering power consumption.
5. It is unclear what hardware was used for the later application demonstrations. If the applications were performed through simulations, the authors should explicitly state this to help readers better assess the significance of the work.
6. How were the input pixels translated into time-series sequences in Figure 2? A more detailed explanation is necessary.

Thank you for your question regarding the definition of the "size of the physical reservoir" in our work. In physical echo state networks (ESNs), the "size of the physical reservoir" (e.g., "500×500") refers to the number of neurons in the physical reservoir, which is directly related to the dimensions of the sparse matrix. The dimensions of the sparse matrix indicate that there are 500 neurons in the physical reservoir, each of which can connect to up to 500 other neurons. 2.2 Does the size of the physical reservoir correspond to the array dimensions of the devices? How are these device arrays fabricated, controlled, and measured? I would suggest that the authors provide a description of the operation of the system.
Thank you for your question regarding the relationship between the physical reservoir size and the device array dimensions, as well as the fabrication, control, and measurement of the device arrays. The size of the physical reservoir directly corresponds to the dimensions of the device array for the English letter recognition and Lorenz attractor tasks. We have added a comprehensive description of the array fabrication, control, and measurement procedures, as well as the overall system operation, in the revised manuscript and supplementary materials to provide greater clarity.
Fabrication of the Device and Array
The bottom gate electrodes were fabricated via physical vapor deposition. Aluminum oxide was subsequently deposited as the gate dielectric using atomic layer deposition. For the semiconductor layers, ZnO was prepared by dissolving the precursor in ammonia to form a uniform solution, while P3HT was dissolved in toluene and thoroughly mixed by stirring and heating to ensure homogeneity. The substrate was placed on a spin coater, and the ZnO precursor solution was dispensed onto it. Spin-coating was performed sequentially at 1500 rpm, 2000 rpm, and 2500 rpm, each for 30 seconds. After spin-coating, the substrate was annealed at 150 °C for 40 minutes to remove the solvent and crystallize the ZnO thin film. The P3HT solution was then applied onto the ZnO layer, with the volume carefully controlled to ensure film uniformity, followed by spin-coating at 1500 rpm for 30 seconds. The resulting film was annealed at 100 °C for 20 minutes.
Device and array structures were defined by covering the thin film with a mask and depositing electrodes via physical vapor deposition. All fabrication steps were conducted in a nitrogen atmosphere. The completed array was encapsulated by covering it with a quartz glass sheet and sealing the edges with UV-curable adhesive.
Control of the Array
Specific rows are selected by applying a feature signal that connects the input voltage to the drain terminals of all transistors in the chosen row via a digital-to-analog converter (DAC). Simultaneously, specific columns are addressed by applying a column selection signal to the gate terminals of all transistors in the selected column. This addressing scheme enables individual control of each unit within the array, facilitating the implementation of matrix multiplication and activation functions.
Measurement of the Array
A custom program was used to sequentially access and test each node in the array, thereby evaluating the operational performance and stability of the array. To measure the output, a resistor with a known value (1 MΩ) was connected in series at the output terminal of the transistor array, allowing the output current to be converted into a voltage signal for further analysis.

2.2 Does this new design contribute to reducing transistor dimensions or increasing the density of transistors per unit area?
In most neuromorphic computing systems, matrix calculations typically require a pair of devices for each node. One device handles long-term potentiation and the other handles long-term depression, allowing for the computation of both positive and negative values by taking the difference between them. This approach effectively doubles the number of devices needed for matrix computation tasks.R6–R8 In contrast, our device exhibits both n-type and p-type characteristics, enabling simultaneous computation of positive and negative values within a single device. As a result, our design requires only half the number of devices compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, due to the sparsity and specificity of ESN, often only 5%–10% of the nodes are actively involved in computation. Furthermore, the authors report identical performance and confusion matrices for both the two-layer and three-layer networks, which is highly implausible given normal variance in training. To further improve accuracy, we introduced a sparse matrix. As shown in Fig. S41, we constructed a (28×28) matrix in which the entries with a value of 1 represent active devices. These devices perform feature mapping through dynamic mechanisms, and their temporal node mappings across columns are aggregated to form higher-level latent space states. By combining these spatial states with the raw data for recognition by the readout layer, we achieved an accuracy of 89.40%. To further enhance performance, we adopted a -1 and +1 strategy, where -1 represents a negative response mechanism (i.e., the positive response multiplied by -1), and +1 represents a positive response. As shown in Fig. S42, this approach increased the accuracy to 89.42%.
To further boost accuracy, we converted these mappings into voltage signals and leveraged the device’s bipolarity to achieve an additional nonlinear transformation. This nonlinear mapping, which mimics the tanh function through bipolar modulation, resulted in an accuracy improvement to 91.54%, as illustrated in Fig. S43. The device’s bipolarity thus serves as an effective means to enhance data nonlinearity. Seeking further improvement, we expanded the dimension of the sparse matrix from (28, 28) to (28, 280), which increased the accuracy to 92.29%, as shown in Fig. S44. However, when the sparse matrix was further expanded to (28, 560), the accuracy decreased to 91.29%, as shown in Fig. S45.
Given this result, we abandoned the dynamic mechanism and instead flattened the image to construct a sparse matrix of (784, 280) dimensions to assist the bipolar neurons in feature extraction. This approach yielded an accuracy of 89.83%, which was lower than the dynamic mechanism-based result of 92.29%, as shown in Fig. S46.
However, when we further increased the size of the sparse matrix to (784, 800), the accuracy reached 92.30%, nearly matching the result achieved with the dynamic mechanism, as shown in Fig. S47. When the full grayscale values of the MNIST dataset were used, the accuracy improved to 92.81%, as shown in Fig. S48. Finally, by expanding the sparse matrix to 1000 columns and controlling the sparsity at 5%, we achieved our highest accuracy of 94.14%, as shown in Fig. S49.

In addition, the system architecture is different from the conventional reservoir design. Between the input and output, the authors introduce an additional fully connected layer, creating a multi-layer feedforward structure. This design significantly complicates the interpretation of results, as it becomes unclear whether the reported performance is attributable to the reservoir or to the fully connected layer. Given that a standard fully connected neural network is already known to perform very well on MNIST, it is likely that the performance gain originates primarily from this component rather than from the reservoir itself.
To support the role of the reservoir, the authors present results comparing single-layer and two-layer fully connected networks, claiming that their system achieves better accuracy. However, these results are questionable. For one, the reported accuracy of the baseline networks is surprisingly low, far below what is commonly achieved on MNIST. A single-layer fully connected network typically exceeds 90% accuracy, and a two-layer network with sufficient neurons generally surpasses 95%. Furthermore, the authors report identical performance and confusion matrices for both the two-layer and three-layer networks, which is highly implausible given normal variance in training. These inconsistencies suggest that the experiments do not reliably isolate or validate the reservoir’s contribution and may even indicate issues in the experimental procedure itself.
Response:
Thank you for raising these concerns regarding our system architecture and the interpretation of our results. We would like to clarify that the additional layer introduced between the input and output is not a conventional fully connected neural network layer, but rather a linear transformation trained using the least squares method. This approach is fundamentally different from standard feedforward neural networks, which typically employ non-linear activation functions and iterative training algorithms.
Our intention was to isolate and highlight the contribution of the physical reservoir component, rather than to rely on algorithmic enhancements. The linear layers in our system serve only to map the features extracted by the reservoir, without introducing additional nonlinearity. As a result, the observed performance improvements can be attributed to the intrinsic properties of the reservoir devices.
Regarding the baseline results, we acknowledge that the reported accuracies for single-layer and two-layer linear networks are lower than those typically achieved by fully connected neural networks on MNIST. This is because our comparison is based on strictly linear models, without the benefit of non-linear activations or deep learning techniques. To ensure transparency and reproducibility, we have made our code and data publicly available for independent verification.

Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewers for your valuable comments. The issues you raised are very important and have indeed provided directions for further improvement of this study. As you rightly pointed out, our current work primarily focuses on leveraging device characteristics for static computing functions, and exploration in processing dynamic data remains insufficient, which creates a certain gap with the concept of typical physical reservoir computing. In response to this concern, we have made significant additions to the research content during the revision.
We propose a novel paradigm that integrates dynamic and static characteristics. This method introduces a dynamic response mechanism to incorporate temporal attributes into data preprocessing, followed by solving through a physically-inspired Echo State Network (ESN) paradigm. This design effectively overcomes the limitations of traditional static approaches, achieving higher-level performance. On the MNIST handwritten digit dataset and the Fashion-MNIST dataset, the proposed paradigm achieves classification accuracies of 96.98% and 86.67%, respectively. In the task of Lorenz attractor prediction, the Normalized Root Mean Square Error (NRMSE) reaches 0.165%, 0.280%, and 0.206%, demonstrating performance comparable to state-of-the-art algorithms. The computational process and relevant explanations of this paradigm are detailed below.
Fig. R1 4-bit encoding with varying pulse intervals. a 5 ms, b 10 ms, c 15 ms, d 20 ms, e 25 ms, f 30 ms.
We applied a 5 ms pulse voltage to the gate and subsequently measured the I . ds After the pulse was applied, different time intervals were set to achieve varying levels of 4bit computation. A 4bit encoding scheme was adopted, with pulse intervals set at 5 ms, 10 ms, 15 ms, 20 ms, 25 ms, and 30 ms, respectively. As shown in Fig. R1a, when the pulse interval is 5 ms, the device exhibits clear 4bit encoding characteristics, and its 16 distinguishable conductance states can be used for image encoding. However, as shown in Fig.R1b, when the pulse interval is increased to 10 ms, all conductance states except for the unstimulated code "0000" shift toward lower conductance values. This shift introduces distinct feature representations for image processing. When the pulse interval is further increased to 15 ms (Fig. R1c), the conductance states continue to shift toward lower values, indicating that changes in pulse interval alter the device’s response pattern.
Taking the code "1110" as an example for analysis: when the pulse interval is 5 ms, the drain current at the first recorded point (Step 1) is approximately 39.95 nA, while at the last recorded point (Step 4) it is approximately 53.00 nA. When the interval increases to 10 ms, the Step 1 current decreases to 38.70 nA, and Step 4 decreases to 48.64 nA. At 15 ms, Step 1 is 37.45 nA and Step 4 is 39.30 nA. As observed in these three cases, the Step 1 current consistently remains higher than that of Step 4, but the gap between them gradually narrows. This indicates that the first three pulses significantly influence the output of the last pulse, and this influence weakens as the interval increases. This trend reverses when the pulse interval reaches 20 ms (Fig. R1d). Here, the Step 1 current is 35.93 nA, while Step 4 is 35.37 nA, meaning Step 1 begins to fall below Step 4. As the interval further increases to 25 ms (Fig. R1e) and 30 ms (Fig. R1f), the Step 1 currents are 35.28 nA and 34.41 nA, respectively, while Step 4 decreases further to 31.59 nA and 29.70 nA, gradually widening the gap between them.
These changes demonstrate that the influence of the first three pulses on the last pulse gradually diminishes as the pulse interval increases. The current response at the final time step transitions from being predominantly shaped by the collective effect of the preceding pulses to being more independently governed by the last pulse itself.
This shift in the dynamic response mechanism provides the system with new opportunities to learn and map image features from different perspectives.
Fig. R2 Mapping of the digital number 5 using different pulse intervals.
The 4-bit encoding mapping method was adopted, where each row of 28 elements is divided into 7 regions and mapped using 4-bit encoding. The original binarized data exhibits significant differences after mapping. Since the image is divided into 196 subregions, the data acquires a temporal dimension after undergoing the dynamic response transformation of the device. Different pulse intervals lead to distinct mapping patterns, with variations not only in the range of conductance values but also in the differentiated presentation of local features.
To facilitate understanding, we take the red-marked region in the figure as an example. The corresponding encoding for this region is "1000". It can be observed that at a time interval of 5 ms, the conductance of this region gradually decays over time and stands out clearly against the background. However, when the time interval increases to 10 ms, the features of this region weaken significantly. Further increasing the interval to 15 ms, the I at Step 4 becomes similar to the background, indicating a noticeable degree of decay. This shows that the mapping characteristics at this point differ markedly from those at 5 ms.
As the time interval continues to increase, this trend becomes more pronounced. At an interval of 20 ms, the I at Step 3 begins to lose distinctiveness; by 25 ms, the I at Step 2 also becomes blurred; and when the interval reaches 30 ms, the I at Step 2 is already difficult to clearly discern. Thus, the dynamic response mechanism can effectively process image features, enhancing the diversity and hierarchical richness of the data. When applied to image recognition tasks, the system can leverage the features exhibited during the dynamic response process as a reference, thereby improving the accuracy and robustness of image recognition.
Due to the distinct boundary between the digits and the background, when encoding is used for mapping, the involvement of codes other than pure "0000" or "1111" tends to yield richer feature variations. The reason is that when only "0000" and "1111" are involved, the encoding merely reflects the maximum and minimum values of the I . In contrast, when boundaries are present, the system through its dynamic response mechanism can generate a greater diversity of feature expression possibilities.
Fig. R3 Mapping of the shoe using different pulse intervals.
On the Fashion dataset, although the overall situation is similar to that described earlier, the elements in this dataset are inherently denser. After binarization, compared to the handwritten digits dataset, it exhibits fewer edge features. Despite the presence of the dynamic response mechanism, due to the relatively similar structure of the elements within the dataset, the expressive differences remain rather limited. For instance, when the pulse interval was set to 5 ms, we applied the same method for mapping and obtained corresponding results. However, since most of the image content occupies the main area of the 28 × 28 pixel grid, the corresponding subset patterns are highly similar. When the time interval was increased to 10 ms, the output only showed a lightening of color, indicating that this is essentially a data scaling operation. Further increasing the interval to 15 ms resulted in continued fading of the color, but no significant new features generated by the dynamic response were observed. Thus, it can be concluded that the dynamic response provides only limited improvement in enhancing the feature representation capability for this dataset.
Fig. R4 Reservoir states of a physical ESN output for different pulse intervals. a digits dataset, b fashion dataset.
We utilize ambipolar transistors to construct a sparse matrix and a tanh function, which together form a high-dimensional, sparsely coupled nonlinear dynamical system. In this system, the sparse matrix defines the topology of information propagation and multi-scale memory pathways, while the tanh function introduces saturating nonlinearity, confining the system dynamics within a bounded range. The synergistic interaction between the two generates rich separated states and gradually decaying memory properties, thereby providing an analytically tractable dynamical foundation for temporal information processing.
Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed physical dynamic preprocessing method effectively achieves high-dimensional nonlinear mapping of data. When the physically preprocessed data is fed into the physically implemented Echo State Network (ESN) system, the reservoir states naturally exhibit a balanced and separable spatial distribution. This effectively avoids common issues such as neuron saturation or degradation often observed in traditionally randomly initialized reservoirs, significantly enhancing feature discriminability and system interpretability. As shown in Fig. R4a and Fig. R4b, which present the spatial distributions of partial reservoir states for the handwritten digit dataset and the Fashion dataset, respectively, the state values are predominantly concentrated within the interval [-0.1, 0.1]. This indicates that the system operates in the approximately linear region of the tanh function, maintaining dynamic stability while retaining sufficient nonlinear expressive capability. Further analysis reveals that the physical ESN essentially projects the input mapping into a higher-dimensional feature space, after which effective classification can be achieved using only a simple linear classifier, with excellent performance. This aligns with the fundamental idea of Cover's theorem—data in high-dimensional spaces are more easily linearly separable—which structurally explains the superior performance of the physical ESN. Moreover, leveraging the dynamic response of ambipolar transistors for image preprocessing essentially integrates the dynamic characteristics of the physical system with nonlinear computational mechanisms, offering a viable pathway toward efficient and low-power neuromorphic computing.
Fig. R5 MNIST datasets accuracy by jointly utilizing six reservoir spatial states. a digits datasets, b fashion datasets.
We employ dynamic response systems with different parameters to map input images, forming multiple feature extraction pathways. Distinctive features are extracted from the reservoir states of each pathway, each reflecting the projection characteristics of the input image under different physical dynamic mechanisms. Subsequently, all multi-path features are concatenated and fused, and then fed into a simple classifier for joint recognition.
The experimental results demonstrate that this method effectively enhances classification performance. On the handwritten digit dataset and the Fashion dataset, classification accuracies reach 96.98% and 86.67%, respectively (as shown in Figures a and b). In particular, the 4-bit preprocessed data achieved through varying pulse widths, when further processed by a physical ESN, significantly improves classification accuracy. The underlying principle is that multi-parameter preprocessing generates diverse feature mappings. Compared to the original single image, these mappings express richer structural information from multiple dynamic dimensions, thereby enhancing feature discriminability and robustness.
Fig. R6 Lorenz attractor mappings under different pulse intervals along the x, y, and z axes. a x axes, b y axes and c z axes.
We model the dynamic response of the transistor as an intrinsic kinetic process. When the chaotic time-series signal of the Lorenz system, such as x(t), is normalized and applied as a gate voltage input, the charge transport and storage mechanisms within the device introduce a memory superposition effect of historical states. As a result, the real-time I reflects not only the current input but also the influence of past signals. In the experiment, pulse sequences with different time intervals (5-25 ms) were used for excitation and readout to probe the dynamic memory characteristics of the device. Fig. R6a presents the measurement results along the x axis: under short-interval pulse excitation (5 ms), the I response exhibits sharp peaks, indicating that the device retains significant memory of recent inputs. When the pulse interval is extended to 10 ms, the amplitude of the Ids response weakens noticeably. As the pulse interval further increases to 25 ms, the response further decays and the features become increasingly smooth. This phenomenon is also observed along the y and z axes, demonstrating that the memory effect of the device is time dependent: under short time intervals, the output is strongly correlated with historical signals; as the interval lengthens, this historical correlation gradually diminishes.
Based on the above dynamics, the transient responses collected from the device construct a state sequence driven by nonlinear charge-carrier kinetics. This mechanism naturally performs nonlinear embedding and feature expansion of the input Lorenz signal along the temporal dimension, endowing the resulting data with inherent temporal structure and dynamic information. Consequently, this representation not only preserves the time evolution characteristics of the system but also provides a physically rich input space for subsequent nonlinear decoding and modeling.
The three-dimensional trajectory data (x, y, z) of the Lorenz attractor were normalized to match the dynamic range of the target hardware system. Subsequently, the normalized signals were linearly converted into corresponding analog voltage signals. Finally, through a transconductance circuit or an equivalent conversion module, the voltage signals were further transformed into current signals with explicit temporal evolution characteristics, serving as time‑series driving sources for subsequent processing. Fig. R6a, b and c respectively show the driven results of the x‑, y‑, and z‑axes under different pulses. These temporal current signals drive the physical device at their respective pulse intervals, inducing distinct nonlinear responses in the system.
Fig. R7 Reservoir spatial states corresponding to different pulse intervals for the x, y, and z axes.
Leakage rate (forgetting factor) is the core of ESN for time series prediction tasks. When there is no leakage rate (α=1), the reservoir state is completely overwritten by a new nonlinear transformation at each time step, forming rapidly changing discrete dynamical states. By introducing a leakage rate (0<α<1), the state update becomes a combination of linear mixing of old and new information with nonlinear transformation, equivalent to applying low-pass filtering and inertial smoothing to the reservoir dynamics. This results in continuous state trajectories with adjustable memory time constants—smaller α values lead to slowly evolving long-term memory, suitable for handling slowly varying continuous signals.
By introducing the forgetting factor earlier, we endowed the system with both short-term and long-term memory behaviors. Consequently, its reservoir state space is continuous. With the introduction of the leakage rate (forgetting factor), the reservoir state update transitions from discrete jumps to continuous evolution, thereby acquiring dynamically tunable short- and long-term memory characteristics. This continuity causes the reservoir state trajectories to manifest as smooth, inertial flows in phase space rather than discontinuous jumps. Specifically, each dimension of the state vector becomes a dynamical variable with exponentially decaying memory, whose time constant is directly controlled by the leakage rate. This continuous dynamic not only better simulates the evolution processes of real physical systems (such as neural membrane potentials or circuit transient responses) but also naturally encodes temporal derivative information of the input signals into the reservoir states.
Based on our design modifications, we have redefined the role of the physical ESN, moving away from “simulating the evolution of physical systems” and instead emphasizing its core function as a nonlinear transformer. Under this framework, the system’s temporal characteristics are no longer explicitly generated by the physical ESN’s own state dynamics but originate from the preprocessing coupling between the original time-series signals of the Lorenz attractor and the device’s dynamic characteristics.
Specifically, the chaotic time-series signals (x(t), y(t), z(t)) of the Lorenz system are first applied as excitation inputs to an ambipolar transistor. The device’s inherent nonlinear transconductance characteristics, carrier recombination dynamics, and the electron-hole competition mechanism regulated by the gate voltage collectively form a complex dynamic preprocessing layer. This process transforms the original deterministic Lorenz trajectories into a set of high-dimensional I response sequences that depend on the physical properties of the device. Although these I data originate from a dynamic system, they constitute a "device-dynamic-feature-encoded" static data stream relative to the input of the physical ESN.
Subsequently, these preprocessed I sequences are fed into a static physical ESN. Here, "static" means that the ESN reservoir itself does not possess time-varying state update mechanisms (i.e., no recurrent connections or leaky integration are introduced). Its role is purely to perform spatial nonlinear projection and feature expansion on the input high-dimensional I signals, forming a fixed-dimensional reservoir state space.
As shown in the figure, the output reservoir states are structurally static high-dimensional point sets, where each point corresponds to a feature vector at a specific time after multiple nonlinear transformations.
Although the final reservoir states are static and do not contain explicit temporal recurrence, the critical time dependencies have been effectively encoded into the statistical structure and sequential relationships of the I sequences during the front-end "device dynamic preprocessing" stage. Therefore, this static high-dimensional state space still carries implicit dynamical information about the evolution of the Lorenz system. By training a simple linear readout layer or a lightweight nonlinear decoder, the system can successfully reconstruct and predict the future states of the Lorenz attractor from these static yet information-rich features.
This demonstrates that even with a static reservoir architecture, as long as the front-end preprocessing effectively injects temporal dynamic information, the entire system can still accomplish complex chaotic time-series prediction tasks.
Fig. R8 Prediction results of the Lorenz attractor by the physical ESN under different pulse intervals.
By preprocessing raw time-series data through dynamic characteristics and then solving it via static nonlinear transformations, excellent predictive performance can still be achieved. The dynamic preprocessing stage encodes the temporal evolution characteristics and physical constraints of the system into a high-dimensional feature space, while the subsequent static nonlinear transformation focuses on extracting separable patterns from these features. Specifically, the dynamic processing converts temporal dependencies into spatially distributed statistical features through the transient responses of devices or analog circuits. Subsequently, the static nonlinear layer adjusts the dimensions and separates the patterns of these features, ultimately enabling the reconstruction of system dynamics through linear readout. This "dynamic encoding–static decoding" architecture not only reduces reliance on recurrent computational resources but also demonstrates that temporal information can be transformed into spatial features through preprocessing, thereby enabling the modeling and prediction of dynamic systems within a static framework.
As shown in the figure, despite the clear reconstruction of the Lorenz attractor’s topological structure across different data collection time intervals, the predicted trajectories still exhibit subtle distortions and local deviations. This phenomenon can be attributed to the modeling strategy of "predicting the state at t+2 using the state at t". While the longer prediction step validates the model’s generalization ability, it also amplifies the extreme sensitivity of chaotic systems to initial conditions (i.e., the butterfly effect). In the physical reservoir composed of ambipolar transistors, this sensitivity is further modulated by device non-idealities, leading to cumulative prediction errors manifested as trajectory jitter or slight morphological distortions of the attractor in phase space.
These results are comparable to those obtained by introducing a leakage factor, at least indicating the effectiveness of our approach. Furthermore, when reservoir features extracted from five different pulse intervals are used for prediction, the results become significantly smoother.
Fig. R9 NRMSE under different pulse intervals.
The NRMSE of the predictions across the three Lorenz system dimensions reveals distinct characteristics regarding the influence of pulse interval duration. On the x‑axis, the total prediction error (i.e., the combined error across all intervals) is the highest, with an NRMSE value of 0.23%, indicating that the x‑dimension dynamics are the most challenging to reconstruct under the current modeling setup. On the y‑axis, predictions for the 5 ms, 20 ms, and 25 ms intervals exhibit relatively higher errors, with NRMSE values of 0.745%, 0.846%, and 0.862% respectively, suggesting that the y‑dynamics are particularly sensitive to both very short and long pulse intervals. In the z‑dimension, the highest NRMSE occurs at the shortest pulse interval (5 ms) with a value of 0.799%, reflecting that the faster sampling may inadequately capture the slower-scale variations characteristic of the z‑variable in the Lorenz system. Overall, these results highlight that prediction accuracy is not only dimension-dependent but also closely tied to the temporal sampling strategy, with excessively short or long intervals leading to increased reconstruction errors in specific dynamical components.
To better align with the reviewers’ feedback and emphasize the core contribution, we have revised the manuscript title to “Physical echo state network based on the nonlinearity and dynamic response of ambipolar heterostructure transistors”. We believe this computing paradigm is novel and offers greater suitability and potential for time-series and image processing tasks compared to conventional reservoir computing approaches.

The first adopts the forgetting‑factor method commonly used in ESNs (Supplementary Fig. S28), where the factor α substitutes for explicit dynamic mechanisms. By tuning α, the physical ESN achieves normalized root‑mean‑square errors (NRMSE) of 0.165%, 0.28%, and 0.206% along the x‑, y‑, and z‑axes, respectively. The device’s dynamic response performs nonlinear transformation on the Lorenz attractor, and the resulting time‑varying Ids serves as input to the ESN (Fig. 4b–d). By varying the sampling intervals during preprocessing, different dynamic features can be extracted for prediction. Though the reservoir states under this method appear discrete, they retain encoded temporal information (Supplementary Fig. S32). This preprocessing strategy yields NRMSE values of 0.165%, 0.28%, and 0.206% on the x‑, y‑, and z‑axes, respectively (Fig. 4e)—performance that closely matches, and in some dimensions slightly exceeds, that of the forgetting‑factor method.
